nodes.label: Constans II, first themes
nodes.full: Constans II inherited an empire that had lost Syria and Egypt and from the 640s met the Arab raids with armies settled in districts of Anatolia, the themes, named after the field armies — Armeniakon, Anatolikon, Opsikion — whose commanders ruled their regions. He moved to the West in 662 and was murdered in Syracuse.
nodes.src: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6133–6160; Walter Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992); John Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990).

nodes.label: The theme system
nodes.full: The field armies were settled in districts, the themes, where the soldiers received land or support from the local population and the general became the governor. By the end of the seventh century there were four or five in Anatolia, and in the eighth they were split up. The system turned the army into a militia tied to the soil and made the frontier defence local.
nodes.src: Theophanes; Constantine VII, De thematibus; Haldon 1990; Warren Treadgold, Byzantium and Its Army (1995).

nodes.label: Farmer’s Law
nodes.full: The Nomos Georgikos is a short code of rules about village life — field boundaries, damage to crops, stray animals, theft, hired labourers and shepherds — with fines and, for serious offences, mutilation. It gives a view of a countryside of free peasant communities, of small plots and communal pasture, in the age of the Arab raids.
nodes.src: Nomos Georgikos, ed. Walter Ashburner, Journal of Hellenic Studies 30 (1910); Paul Lemerle, The Agrarian History of Byzantium (1979).

nodes.label: Peasants of the Law
nodes.full: The economy of the Anatolian themes depended on free peasants on small plots in village communities, on pastoralism and on the soldiers' farms. The state's land tax and the villagers' joint liability held the system together. The monasteries and the great estates of the later period were still small.
nodes.src: Farmer's Law; Lemerle 1979; Michael Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985).

nodes.label: Arab raids on Anatolia
nodes.full: After the conquest of Syria, the armies of Muawiya and his generals raided across the Taurus almost every year, reaching Caesarea in 646, Amorion and Chrysopolis, and taking Cyprus and Rhodes from the sea. Byzantium kept its cities but lost the countryside, which was left to be raided.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6137–6180; Michael the Syrian; Kaegi 1992.

nodes.label: Taurus frontier
nodes.full: The Taurus and Anti-Taurus mountains became the border between the caliphate and Byzantium for two centuries. Between the fortified districts lay a no-man's land of burned villages, abandoned fields and fortified passes, where both sides raided and the Byzantines made a policy of avoiding pitched battles.
nodes.src: Haldon and Kennedy 1980; John Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World (1999).

nodes.label: Constantine IV, Justinian II
nodes.full: Constantine IV held the capital against the first Arab blockade and made the Thirty Years' Peace of 678. His son Justinian II settled Slavs in Bithynia, lost his throne in 695, had his nose cut and returned in 705 with Bulgarian help to rule with a terror that ended in his execution in 711.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6161–6203; Nikephoros, Breviarium 36–45.

nodes.label: First siege of Constantinople
nodes.full: An Arab fleet took the Marmara islands and blockaded the city in a series of campaigns over several summers. Greek fire burned the Arab ships, the walls held, and Muawiya sued for a thirty-year peace and a tribute. Some modern historians think the traditional dates mean a series of raids and not one siege.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6165–6170; Nikephoros 34; John Haldon and Hugh Kennedy, Regional Studies in Byzantium (1980).

nodes.label: Greek fire
nodes.full: Kallinikos, an engineer from Heliopolis in Syria, came to Constantinople and showed Constantine IV a weapon: an incendiary liquid, probably based on petroleum, projected through bronze siphons from ships and walls, which burned on water. Its use against the Arab fleet in 674 to 678 is traditionally said to have saved the city. Its composition was a state secret.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6165; John Haldon and Maurice Byrne, 'A possible solution to the problem of Greek fire', Byzantinische Zeitschrift 70 (1977).

nodes.label: Sebastopolis
nodes.full: Justinian II broke the peace and marched against Muhammad ibn Marwan with an army that included thousands of Slavs. At the battle at Sebastopolis in Pontus the Slav commander, bribed by the Arabs, deserted with 20,000 men, and the Byzantines were routed. The emperor took revenge by massacring the Slavs of Bithynia.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6183–6184; Nikephoros 38.

nodes.label: Slavs in Bithynia
nodes.full: After his Balkan campaigns of 688–689, Justinian II moved tens of thousands of Slavs into the Opsikion theme in Bithynia, where they were recruited as soldiers. After their desertion at Sebastopolis, many were killed; the remainder were absorbed. A Slavic settlement in northwest Anatolia is known from place names.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6180–6184; Nikephoros 38; Haldon 1990.

nodes.label: Leo III, Constantine V
nodes.full: Leo, a general of the Anatolikon theme, took power in 717 on the eve of the Arab siege, repelled it and founded a dynasty. His son Constantine V, a military reformer and the greatest soldier of his time, went on to win victories in Syria and Armenia and over the Bulgars, and forbade the veneration of icons. Later iconophiles remembered him as an arch-heretic.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6209–6267; Nikephoros, Breviarium; Paul Speck, Kaiser Konstantin VI (1978); Stephen Gero on Leo III and Constantine V.

nodes.label: Second siege
nodes.full: Maslama led a great Arab army and fleet against Constantinople in the first year of Leo III. The walls, Greek fire, a hard winter that killed many Arabs, and Bulgar attacks on their land forces broke the siege after a year. Arab expansion in Europe stopped at the Bosphorus and the Taurus.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6209–6210; Nikephoros 52–54; Marius Canard on the sieges.

nodes.label: Akroinon
nodes.full: Leo III and his son Constantine met a large Arab raiding force in Phrygia and won a victory at Akroinon, killing the Arab commander. The battle restored the army's confidence and put an end to the large Arab raids that had come almost every year for a century.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6232; Nikephoros 58; Haldon 1990.

nodes.label: Constantine V in Armenia
nodes.full: Taking advantage of the civil war in the caliphate, Constantine V invaded northern Syria in 746 and took Germanikeia, and in 751–752 took and razed Melitene and Theodosiopolis (Erzurum). The inhabitants were moved to Thrace. It was the first Byzantine offensive across the Taurus since the 630s.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6238, 6243; Nikephoros 66.

nodes.label: People moved to Thrace
nodes.full: When Constantine V took Germanikeia in 746 and Melitene and Theodosiopolis in 751–752, he moved Syrian and Armenian Christians, many of them Monophysite and Paulician, to Thrace as a way of repopulating the countryside and of fortifying the Balkan frontier. The Paulicians of Thrace remained for centuries.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6237, 6243; Nikephoros 66.

nodes.label: Ecloga
nodes.full: The Ecloga, issued in the names of Leo III and Constantine V, was a short handbook of Justinian's law in Greek, reworked with the aim of making justice more humane and more Christian. It reformed marriage, inheritance and property law and used mutilation as a substitute for the death penalty.
nodes.src: Ecloga, ed. Burgmann (1983); Gero 1973.

nodes.label: Ban on icons
nodes.full: In the 720s and 730s Leo III, urged by Anatolian bishops who thought the veneration of images was idolatrous, removed the image of Christ over the Chalke Gate and ordered the icons to be taken down. Constantine V called the council at Hieria in 754, which condemned the making and worship of icons. The ban lasted, with a pause, until 843.
nodes.src: Council of Hieria acts (quoted in Nicaea II, Mansi 13); Theophanes AM 6218; Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era (2011).

nodes.label: Women at the Chalke
nodes.full: When the emperor's officer climbed a ladder to remove the icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate, a crowd of women pulled the ladder down and killed him. The emperor had many of them punished. The story is told by iconophile sources, and shows the role of women in the defence of the images.
nodes.src: Life of Stephen the Younger; Theophanes AM 6218; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Nicaea II
nodes.full: Irene and the patriarch Tarasius summoned some 350 bishops to Nicaea in 787 for the seventh ecumenical council, which reversed Hieria and restored the veneration of icons, distinguishing it from the worship due to God alone. The decision was overturned again in 815.
nodes.src: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (Mansi 12–13); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Cross of Hagia Eirene
nodes.full: In the apse of Hagia Eirene, which an earthquake had damaged in 740, Constantine V had a plain black cross set against a gold ground in place of any figural mosaic. It is the main surviving monument of the iconoclast age in the capital and shows an art of ornament and symbol.
nodes.src: Hagia Eirene apse mosaic; Cyril Mango, Byzantine Architecture (1976); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Khazar marriage
nodes.full: In about 732 Leo III married his son Constantine to Tzitzak, daughter of the Khazar khagan, to seal an alliance against the Arabs in the Caucasus. She was baptised as Irene. Her son became the emperor Leo IV, 'the Khazar', and she introduced a Khazar fashion at court, the tzitzakion.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6224; Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De ceremoniis 2.40; Peter Golden, Khazar Studies (1980).

nodes.label: Plague of 747
nodes.full: A new outbreak of bubonic plague spread from Sicily and Calabria into Greece and reached Constantinople in 747, killing so many that the city was repopulated with settlers from Greece and the Aegean islands. The state lost people, taxpayers and soldiers in an age of already small numbers.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6238–6240; Nikephoros 66.

nodes.label: Irene, Nikephoros I
nodes.full: Irene ruled as regent for her son Constantine VI, restored the icons at Nicaea in 787 and in 797 blinded him and reigned in her own name as basileus. She was deposed in 802 by her finance minister, Nikephoros I, who reformed the taxes and died in Bulgaria in 811.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6272–6303; Judith Herrin, Women in Purple (2001).

nodes.label: Irene the empress
nodes.full: Irene, an Athenian by birth, was empress and regent for ten years and in 797 had her son Constantine VI blinded and ruled as basileus, signing her laws with the male title. She was the first woman to rule the empire alone. She was deposed in 802 by her treasurer and sent to a convent on Lesbos.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6289–6295; Judith Herrin, Women in Purple (2001).

nodes.label: Seven vexations
nodes.full: Nikephoros I, a finance minister turned emperor, took in the plunder of the Church, imposed a hearth tax, made the villagers jointly liable for the taxes of their neighbours who fled (the allelengyon), and taxed the Church's lands. The hostile chronicler Theophanes counted them as the seven vexations. They stabilised the state's finances.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6302; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Pliska
nodes.full: Nikephoros I led a large army into Bulgaria, took and burned the capital Pliska, but was trapped in the mountains and killed with most of his officers. Krum, the khan, had his skull lined with silver and used as a drinking cup. The Byzantine army of Thrace and Anatolia was shattered.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6303; Scriptor incertus de Leone; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Harun’s invasions
nodes.full: In 782 Harun, then a prince, led an army across Anatolia to Chrysopolis, opposite Constantinople, and obliged Irene to pay tribute. As caliph he took Heraclea and Tyana in 806 and forced Nikephoros I to pay again. The caliph's ransoming of Roman prisoners became an annual affair.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6274, 6298; Tabari.

nodes.label: Theophanes
nodes.full: Theophanes, a monk who founded a monastery at Megas Agros in Bithynia, completed the chronicle begun by his friend George Syncellus. The Chronographia, a year-by-year account from 284 to 813, is the main source for the seventh and eighth centuries and is written from the iconophile point of view.
nodes.src: Theophanes, Chronographia, ed. de Boor (1883); Cyril Mango and Roger Scott (trans., 1997).

nodes.label: Breviarium
nodes.full: Nikephoros, a civil servant who became patriarch in 806, wrote a short history of the empire from 602 to 769 in a clear style, using good sources. With Theophanes it is one of the two main accounts of the dark age of Byzantium.
nodes.src: Nikephoros, Breviarium historicum, ed. Mango (1990).

nodes.label: Theodore the Studite
nodes.full: Theodore, abbot of Sakkoudion in Bithynia and then of the Stoudios monastery in the capital, made a strict community of monks with a written constitution, a scriptorium and a rule of common life. The Studite reform spread across Byzantium and later Athos. He led the iconophile monks against emperors and was exiled three times.
nodes.src: Theodore the Studite, Letters and Catecheses; Life of Theodore the Studite; Julian Hendrix on Studite monasticism.

nodes.label: Michael II, Theophilus
nodes.full: Michael II, an Amorian officer, killed Leo V in church and founded a dynasty. His son Theophilus, an able and just ruler fond of building and ceremony, fought the caliphs in a war that cost him Amorion and ended with his death in 842, and restored the strength of the state.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 2–3; Genesios; Warren Treadgold, The Byzantine Revival (1988).

nodes.label: Thomas the Slav
nodes.full: Thomas, a general who claimed to be the dead Constantine VI, raised the armies of the East with a promise of tax relief and brought the Anatolian themes, with a fleet, to the walls of Constantinople in December 821. He was defeated, with the help of a Bulgarian army, and executed. Michael II's throne was secured at the cost of an economic and military crisis.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 2.10–20; Genesios 2; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Sack of Amorion
nodes.full: The caliph al-Mu'tasim answered Theophilus's raids by leading a huge army against Amorion, birthplace of the ruling dynasty. Theophilus was beaten at Dazimon in July, and the city fell after a fifteen-day siege through the treachery of a gate commander. The inhabitants were killed or enslaved and forty-two officers were executed in 845. Abu Tammam wrote a poem on the victory.
nodes.src: Tabari; Abu Tammam, Ode on Amorium; Theophanes Continuatus 3.29–38; Life of the 42 Martyrs of Amorion.

nodes.label: Beacon line
nodes.full: A chain of fire-beacons ran from a fortress above the Cilician Gates, Loulon, across Anatolia to the Pharos of the Great Palace, and could carry the news of an Arab raid to the emperor within a few hours. The invention is credited to Leo the Mathematician under Theophilus.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 4.35 (Constantine VII's account); Constantine VII, De ceremoniis (the beacon text).

nodes.label: Throne of Solomon
nodes.full: In the throne hall of the Magnaura palace, Theophilus had a throne with mechanical lions that roared, birds on a golden tree that sang and a throne that rose in the air, made by Leo the Mathematician's craftsmen to impress foreign envoys. Liutprand of Cremona described it a century later.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 3.42; Liutprand of Cremona, Antapodosis 6.5; Constantine VII, De ceremoniis 2.15.

nodes.label: Leo the Mathematician
nodes.full: Leo, a teacher of philosophy and geometry, headed the school established by Bardas at the Magnaura palace in about 855, and was the first of the Byzantine scholars to revive the study of the Greek mathematicians and astronomers. His manuscripts of Euclid, Archimedes and Ptolemy are the base of later copies.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 4.26–29; Paul Lemerle, Byzantine Humanism (1986).

nodes.label: Greek books for Baghdad
nodes.full: Arab sources tell that the caliph al-Ma'mun sent embassies to the Byzantine emperor to obtain manuscripts of Greek philosophers and doctors. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, the leading translator, travelled in the Byzantine lands to find Galen and the other manuscripts. The translation movement in Baghdad depended on Greek books from Byzantium and Syria.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist; Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Risala; Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998).

nodes.label: Lamos exchanges
nodes.full: At the river Lamos on the Cilician border, Byzantines and Arabs exchanged prisoners in elaborate ceremonies, according to Arab and Greek sources, by tens or thousands, with the caliph's envoys on one bank and the emperor's on the other. Exchanges were made in 797, 805, 845, 860 and later. They show a common culture of frontier war.
nodes.src: Tabari; Ya'qubi; Michael the Syrian; Nadia El-Cheikh on Byzantine–Arab diplomacy.

nodes.label: Amorion excavations
nodes.full: Excavations at Amorion show a city that kept walls, a church, baths and streets with workshops through the seventh and eighth centuries and prospered in the ninth, where earlier theories had pictured an empty fortress. The destruction layer of 838 is plain. The picture of an Anatolian dark age needs qualification.
nodes.src: Chris Lightfoot (ed.), Amorium Reports I–III (1997–2012); Chris Lightfoot and Eric Ivison, Amorium: A Byzantine City in Anatolia (2012).

nodes.label: Michael III, Theodora, Bardas
nodes.full: Michael III was two when his father died, and the empire was run by his mother Theodora, who restored the icons in 843, and then from 856 by her brother Bardas, a patron of learning, until Basil, a groom promoted to co-emperor, killed Bardas in 866 and Michael in 867.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 4; Symeon Logothete; Photius, Letters; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Triumph of Orthodoxy
nodes.full: The regent Theodora, with the patriarch Methodios and a synod, restored the veneration of icons on the first Sunday of Lent in 843. The Church still keeps the day as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. The late emperor Theophilus was exonerated in a story that she said that he had kissed an icon before dying.
nodes.src: Life of Theodora; Theophanes Continuatus 4.1–4; Synodikon of Orthodoxy.

nodes.label: Theodora the regent
nodes.full: Theodora, a Paphlagonian by birth, was the widow of Theophilus and ruled for her young son Michael III with the logothete Theoktistos for fourteen years. She restored the icons and held the treasury in good order and was removed to a convent by Bardas in 856.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 4; Symeon Logothete; Herrin 2001.

nodes.label: Chludov Psalter
nodes.full: A psalter made in the capital soon after the end of iconoclasm shows in its margins the iconoclast patriarch John the Grammarian whitewashing an image of Christ, set beside the soldier who offered the Saviour vinegar on a sponge. The book is a polemic in paint by the winners.
nodes.src: Chludov Psalter (State Historical Museum, Moscow, MS gr. 129d); Kathleen Corrigan, Visual Polemics in the Ninth-Century Byzantine Psalters (1992).

nodes.label: Kassia
nodes.full: Kassia, a noblewoman said to have been a candidate at Theophilus's bride-show of 830 and to have lost by a sharp answer, became a nun and founded a convent. Her hymns, including the one for Holy Wednesday on the woman who anointed Christ, are sung in the Orthodox church today. She is the first Byzantine woman composer whose works survive.
nodes.src: Kassia, Hymns and Epigrams (ed. Antonia Tripolitis, 1992); Symeon Logothete (bride-show); Diane Touliatos-Miles.

nodes.label: Photius
nodes.full: Photius, a scholar-statesman who became patriarch in 858, wrote the Bibliotheca, a review in 279 entries of books he had read, with summaries and criticism of pagan and Christian authors. It preserves much of lost Greek literature, including large parts of Ctesias and Diodorus.
nodes.src: Photius, Bibliotheca, ed. René Henry (1959–91); Nigel Wilson, Photius: The Bibliotheca (1994).

nodes.label: Rus attack
nodes.full: In June 860 a fleet of some 200 small ships of the Rus sailed down from the Black Sea and ravaged the suburbs of Constantinople while the emperor and the army were at war with the Arabs. They were gone within weeks. The patriarch Photius preached on the event in two homilies. It is the first time the Rus appear in the Byzantine sources.
nodes.src: Photius, Homilies 3–4; Theophanes Continuatus 4.33; Cyril Mango, The Homilies of Photius (1958).

nodes.label: Cyril and Methodius
nodes.full: The brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius, of Thessalonica, were prepared for their mission to the Slavs at the monastery of Polychron on Mount Olympus in Bithynia, where Methodius was abbot. Cyril devised the Glagolitic alphabet for the Moravian mission in 863. Anatolia's monasteries gave Slavic literacy its first teachers.
nodes.src: Life of Constantine (Cyril) and Life of Methodius (Old Church Slavonic); Francis Dvornik, Byzantine Missions among the Slavs (1970).

nodes.label: Lalakaon
nodes.full: Umar al-Aqta, emir of Melitene, raided as far as the Black Sea coast at Amisus, and was trapped by the Byzantine general Petronas, brother of Bardas, at the Lalakaon river. The emir and most of his army were killed, and Byzantine forces began to take the offensive. It marks the turning point of the frontier war.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus 4.34–35; Tabari; Genesios 4.

nodes.label: Emirs of Melitene and Tarsus
nodes.full: Across the Taurus the Abbasid caliphs kept a line of fortified frontier districts, the thughur, headed by emirs of Melitene (Malatya) and Tarsus, who led summer raids into Anatolia as holy war and winter raids for booty. Their wealth rested on slaves and ransoms. Umar al-Aqta of Melitene and Ali ibn Yahya of Tarsus were the great frontier chiefs of the 9th century.
nodes.src: Tabari; Ya'qubi; Michael the Syrian; Michael Bonner, Aristocratic Violence and Holy War (1996).

nodes.label: The Paulicians
nodes.full: The Paulicians, a Christian sect founded by Constantine-Silvanus of Mananali about the 650s, according to their hostile reporters rejected the Old Testament, the veneration of the Virgin, the cross and the hierarchy, and revered Paul above all. They had lived in the borderlands of Armenia and Pontus and were persecuted by Byzantium. Later they were accused of Manichaean dualism.
nodes.src: Photius, Contra Manichaeos; Peter of Sicily; Nina Garsoïan 1967.

nodes.label: Karbeas and Tephrike
nodes.full: After Theodora's persecution of the Paulicians in 843–844, the officer Karbeas went over to the emir of Melitene with 5,000 followers and built a fortified state at Tephrike, from which he and his successor Chrysocheir raided Asia Minor as far as Ephesus. Basil I destroyed it in 872.
nodes.src: Peter of Sicily, History of the Paulicians; Theophanes Continuatus 4.16–25; Nina Garsoïan, The Paulician Heresy (1967).

nodes.label: Armenians in Byzantium
nodes.full: Armenian nobles and soldiers entered Byzantine service in large numbers from the seventh century, as generals of the Armeniakon theme and then as emperors: Leo V the Armenian (813–820) and, from a family of Armenian descent, Basil I (867). The Byzantine army and court became more Armenian each century.
nodes.src: Nina Garsoïan, 'The Problem of Armenian Integration into the Byzantine Empire', in Angeliki Laiou and Helene Ahrweiler (eds), Studies on the Internal Diaspora of the Byzantine Empire (1998).

nodes.label: Shrinking cities
nodes.full: Under the strain of the Arab and Persian wars and the plague, the big cities of western Anatolia shrank to fortified cores. Ephesus moved up to the hill of Ayasuluk, Sardis kept a small walled area, Pergamon a citadel and Ankara a walled enclosure on its citadel. Late antique urbanism gave way to a landscape of fortresses and villages.
nodes.src: Clive Foss, Ephesus after Antiquity (1979); Foss, Byzantine Fortifications (1986); Mitchell, Anatolia vol. 2.

nodes.label: Trebizond road
nodes.full: Trebizond on the Black Sea coast was the port of a road that ran over the Zigana pass to Armenia and Persia, which carried silks and other goods to the Arab world. Ibn Khurradadhbih in his Book of Roads and Kingdoms of about 846 lists the Byzantine customs. It was a frontier trade in a time of war.
nodes.src: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-masalik wa'l-mamalik; Hendy 1985.

nodes.label: Underground refuges
nodes.full: In the volcanic tuff of Cappadocia people cut multi-storey underground refuges with air shafts, wells, stables, storerooms and rolling stone doors, in which a village could hide for days from the Arab raiders. Derinkuyu has eight levels. Their date is debated, but many were used or extended in the age of the raids.
nodes.src: Lyn Rodley, Cave Monasteries of Byzantine Cappadocia (1985); Ousterhout, Visual Cultures of Cappadocia.

nodes.label: The Arab conquests begin
nodes.full: After the Prophet’s death in 632 the caliphs’ armies took Syria, Mesopotamia, Egypt and Persia within a generation and reached the Taurus.
nodes.src: background — see the Caliphate 632–750 folio (caliphate-632-750) and the Late Roman Anatolia folio (late-roman-anatolia-330-632)
